title: Benchmark & Profile

answers: Rewrite the hot loop from intuition
writing.exampleCaption: The example makes the contract visible in code.
writing.explanation:
A benchmark measures a stable workload; a profiler explains where its time or allocations go. Change one variable, protect against optimized-away work, and compare distributions rather than one lucky run.

A benchmark asks how a specific workload behaves under controlled conditions. A profiler asks where time, allocations, or waits occur during that workload. Start with a question that matters to a user, such as median parse latency for a typical file or worst-case response time for a large project. Use a release build, warm up when appropriate, and keep input, hardware, and environment stable between comparisons. One `Instant` measurement is useful for a quick observation but too noisy to settle a small optimization.

A compiler may remove work whose result is unused, so a benchmark must keep the result observable; `black_box` can help prevent an obvious optimization in a microbenchmark but does not make the benchmark realistic by itself. Record a distribution over repeated runs and look for variance from caching, scheduling, and I/O. Profile the slow case before changing code. If allocations dominate, reserve capacity or borrow data; if the algorithm scales poorly, a container or complexity change may matter more. Change one variable, rerun the same workload, and keep a correctness test. Report both the improvement and its cost in memory, code complexity, or startup time.

For a before-and-after report, include the input shape, sample count, median and slower-tail observations, build mode, and what you held constant. If the result is within the noise, say so. A useful profile names the expensive path and gives enough context to reproduce it; a colorful flame graph without a workload description is not an engineering conclusion.
